items.title: Morning Briefing: Nov. 6, 2026
items.excerpt: Here’s a rundown of all the news you need to start your Friday, including US President Donald Trump warning that Iran could face further destruction, Türkiye’s parliament approving a trilateral defense pact with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, and Israel's president to announce Sunday who will be tasked with forming government. US President Donald Trump said he may have to “destroy the rest” of Iran and that “you’ll know soon enough.” “Now we’ll make a decision: Do we want to go further and just certify it, by certifying it meaning it will never happen again?” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. “I would rather not destroy the rest of the country, if possible, but maybe I’ll have to. And you’ll know soon enough,” he said. Trump also dismissed speculation that he is considering replacing Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, stating that “he’s doing a very good job.” - Turkish parliament approves Mecca joint defense pact with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia The Turkish parliament approved a bill ratifying the Mecca Agreement on Joint Defense between Türkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, clearing the way for the trilateral security pact to take effect. Lawmakers endorsed the measure by 279 votes to 119, with 398 of the chamber’s 592 members taking part in the ballot. During the debate, ruling Justice and Development (AK) Party lawmaker Ziya Altunyaldiz stressed that the agreement aims to expand security cooperation in the region. He emphasized that it contains no approach against any third country and that its main goal is to prevent conflicts rather than escalate them. - Israel's president to announce Sunday who will be tasked with forming government Israel’s president said he will announce Sunday which lawmaker will be tasked with forming the next government following consultations with political parties following last month’s elections. In a Thursday video message reported by Israeli news outlet Ynet, Isaac Herzog said parties representing 67 members of the 120-seat Knesset recommended Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot, while parties holding 46 seats backed current Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, leader of the Likud party. “The results of the consultations may appear clear,” Herzog said, but added that the ability to form a government remains uncertain due to mutual objections between and within political blocs. He said he would hold further individual talks with party leaders to assess their prospects of forming a coalition. Herzog stressed that he would make every effort to facilitate the formation of a stable government.

items.title: Headlines for November 06, 2026 | Democracy Now!
items.excerpt: ## Democrats Lead in Alaska and Mississippi Senate Races as House Majority Approaches 260 Seats Nov 06, 2026 Democrats continue to build on their historic gains in Tuesday’s midterm elections as final results are tabulated. So far, Democrats have won 253 House seats compared to Republicans’ 157, with 25 races still undecided. In Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom has added to his narrow lead over incumbent Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith. He’s currently ahead by more than 1,800 votes as election officials process provisional ballots and late-arriving mail ballots. Colom would be the first Black senator from Mississippi since Blanche K. Bruce was elected in 1875, during the Reconstruction era. In Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola narrowly leads incumbent Republican Senator Dan Sullivan by just over 600 votes, though a quarter of ballots remain to be counted. If Democrats win Alaska and Mississippi, their Senate caucus will grow to 56 members. ... ## Pete Hegseth Defends Iran War, Demands $350B in Additional Funding and Vows to Fight Impeachment Nov 06, 2026 Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth defended the Iran war and lashed out at his critics on Thursday, as the House of Representatives prepares to vote as early as next week on articles of impeachment. The effort to oust Hegseth is being led by Kentucky’s outgoing Republican Congressmember Thomas Massie, who gave Hegseth an ultimatum after Tuesday’s historic losses for Republicans: Resign or be removed by Congress. The effort appears to have enough bipartisan support to pass, after many Republican lawmakers turned on Hegseth following their party’s election rout. On Thursday, Hegseth posted a defiant video on social media in which he lavished praise on President Trump, demanded at least $350 billion in additional military funding, said transgender troops have a mental illness incompatible with military service, and claimed victory over diversity, equity and inclusion, which he called a “Marxist ideology built to destroy us.” And Hegseth vowed to fight against impeachment.

items.excerpt: ## Latino voters swing left in midterm elections, lifting Democrats to big wins in Texas and nationwide SAN JUAN, Texas (AP) — Latino voters moved sharply to the left in the midterm elections, helping Democrats achieve significant victories in Texas and in key House races nationwide. This marks a change for a demographic that had been leaning right for nearly a decade. Hispanic voters, especially those in the working class, have been impacted by economic challenges, leading them to reject President Donald Trump and his Republican Party. Latinos also have been especially affected by Trump’s immigration crackdown. Democrats focused on cost-of-living issues, gaining support. In Texas, every county voted more Democratic than in 2024. However, experts warn this shift may not be permanent as it depends on Democrats fulfilling campaign promises. ## AI data centers took a beating in the midterm elections. A reckoning may be ahead for tech giants HARRISBURG, Pa. (AP) — Opposition to artificial intelligence data centers was part of midterm races across the U.S., with campaigns featuring them in hundreds of millions of dollars' worth of TV ads and many winners pledging to clamp down on the energy-hungry behemoths. A tougher regulatory environment for tech giants and data center developers is expected to follow, even if President Donald Trump — perhaps the industry’s biggest champion — stalls any federal crackdown. Data center regulation itself was not on most midterm ballots, but hard-line stances against the server warehouses were woven into the platforms of Democrats who upended longtime Republican control of the governorships in Texas, Ohio and Georgia, all data center hot spots. ... ## Ukrainian President Zelenskyy presses Western allies for clear postwar security guarantees KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says his government is seeking specific security guarantees from Western allies for post-war support. His comments came after two days of discussions in Brussels focusing on post-war security and reconstruction. ... ## US employers added a surprising 165,000 jobs in October; unemployment rate dipped to 4.1% WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. employers created a surprising 165,000 new jobs last month, and the unemployment rate dipped to 4.1%. The hiring beat the 65,000 new jobs forecasters had expected. The jobs report comes three days after voters delivered stunning defeat to President Donald Trump and his Republican Party in midterm elections. Frustrated with the state of the economy — and especially the high cost of living – Americans handed full control of Congress to the Democrats. ## The worldwide sell-off for AI stocks halts, but other US stocks are still struggling NEW YORK (AP) — AI stocks are bouncing back and recovering some of their brutal sell-off. The rest of the U.S. stock market, though, is lagging behind Friday following a whirlwind few days of Wall Street trying to sort out what this week’s U.S. midterm elections will mean for the economy. The S&P 500 rose 0.3% to trim its loss for the week. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 476 points, and the Nasdaq composite rallied 1.1%. The relative steadiness for Wall Street halted what had been a worldwide tumble for stocks. Treasury yields ticked higher following a strong report on U.S. hiring.

items.title: US inflation too high; essential to get back to 2%: Fed’s Williams By Reuters
items.excerpt: FRANKFURT, Nov 6 (Reuters) - US economic growth has remained resilient and the labour market is remarkably stable despite successive shocks, but inflation is too high and must be brought back to 2%, New York Federal Reserve President John Williams said on Friday. Inflation has soared across the world, mostly as the US war on Iran has pushed energy prices higher but also because soaring investment in AI has pushed up costs for some IT-related products and services. "Inflation is absolutely too high. It’s been too high for too long," Williams told a European Central Bank conference in Frankfurt. "It’s absolutely essential that we bring inflation back to our 2% target in a timely manner and a sustained basis." But Williams also argued that the Fed’s key focus should be on where inflation is heading and making sure that current shocks do not translate into broader or more persistent inflation. "Fortunately, we’re not seeing that happen so far in terms of inflation expectations, which remain well anchored," Williams said. "We’re seeing wage growth (that is), I think, consistent with our 2% goal." While Williams did not discuss what the Fed’s next policy move should be, he said the bank’s last policy statement had correctly concluded that it was appropriate for the Fed to collect more information to determine what the appropriate stance of policy is. Financial markets see a more than 50% chance of a rate hike by the Fed in December while a move by March is fully priced in.

items.title: U.S. continues to generate jobs, yet inflation is eroding Americans' spending power | PBS News
items.excerpt: WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. employers created a surprising 165,000 new jobs last month, and the unemployment rate dipped to 4.1%. Hiring was far stronger than the 65,000 new jobs that economists had expected. The jobs report comes three days after voters delivered a stunning defeat to President Donald Trump and his Republican Party in midterm elections. Frustrated with the state of the economy — and especially the high cost of living – Americans handed full control of Congress to the Democrats. But the latest jobs report looked solid. Labor Department revisions added a combined 84,000 new jobs to the August and September totals. The unemployment rate fell even though 421,000 people entered the labor force. Average hourly wages rose 0.4% in October from September, the biggest month-over-month gain since January. "This was a blowout jobs report," said Angelo Kourkafas, senior global strategist at Edward Jones. "Payroll growth exceeded expectations, revisions were positive, the unemployment rate fell, participation improved, and wage growth strengthened." The strong job gains will likely make Federal Reserve policymakers more confident in the health of the labor market, giving them leeway to focus on persistently high inflation and raise their benchmark interest rate at their next meeting in December. The central bank typically seeks to bring down inflation by lifting its key interest rate to cool borrowing and spending. The Fed raised the rate in September but left it alone at its meeting last month. Wall Street investors now see the chance of a December rate hike at 77%, up about 10 percentage points from Thursday, according to CME's FedWatch. "For sure, we're looking at another rate increase in December and possibly another one in early 2027," said Boston College economist Brian Bethune. Solid hiring also underscores a concern among many Fed officials that their key rate isn't high enough to slow inflation. Hourly wages were up a meager 3.1% from October 2025. That means many workers have seen their purchasing power decline over the past year, despite continued hiring. ... The American economy and job market have proven resilient in the face of a series of shocks — Trump's double-digit tariffs on imports and the war with Iran, which has driven U.S. gasoline prices above $4 a gallon and pinched family budgets. Gross domestic product — the nation's output of goods and services — advanced at a sprightly 3.4% annual pace from July through September, lifted by strong consumer spending and booming investment in artificial intelligence.

items.title: Fed policymakers consider rate hike after strong jobs report | MarketScreener
items.excerpt: Nov 6 (Reuters) - A stronger-than-expected US jobs report bolstered the case for further Federal Reserve interest rate hikes, which had lost some momentum amid a post-election stock market selloff and growing fears that weaker AI-driven demand could undercut the economy. Employers added 165,000 jobs last month, more than twice what economists had expected, the Bureau of Labor Statistics said on Friday, and the unemployment rate ticked down to 4.1%. Average hourly wages gained 3.1% from a year earlier, not enough to keep up with a 3.7% rise in consumer prices that is taking a bigger chunk of the typical paycheck's purchasing power. After the US central bank left its policy rate on hold last month, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said policymakers would be watching for "the accumulation of data" to help decide whether more monetary policy tightening would be needed. For San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly, the latest monthly jobs report appeared to put a definitive tick in the "yes" column. "People are just at the point where they're -- they say 'Inflation -- I'm doing well in everything, except I can't keep up with inflation,' so that has to be our number one priority, and the fact that we have a solid labor market gives us the latitude, really, to just get that job done," Daly said in an interview on CNBC. "My expectation is, we're going to have to tighten policy further," said Daly, who is not a voting member of the Fed's policy committee this year but typically voices views similar to the majority view. Noting "how volatile the world seems to be in many ways," she added, "those volatilities are something that you have to take into account, collect more information, and be deliberate but more gradual in how you get there when you don't know exactly where you're going to need to head. But more is likely to be needed and certainly we're prepared -- I'm prepared -- to do that, if that's what the economy calls for." In comments at a St. Louis civic event on Friday, St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said inflation remained the top concern in his conversations with businesses in his district. "Inflation is a regressive tax, a distortionary tax," said Musalem, who has advocated for further rate increases. "The best thing we can do for growth and employment is bring inflation back down on a timely basis." He did not address a recent swoon in stock markets driven lower by new doubts about the pace and sustainability of the artificial intelligence boom, but said for now he feels the emerging industry is feeding higher inflation through demand for commodities such as copper. Even if that pays off in future profit and productivity, "we need to make monetary policy for the economy of the day, not what it may be five years from now," Musalem said, and on that basis, for now at least, AI investment "will continue to contribute to inflation." ... Markets were pricing about an 80% chance of a quarter-percentage-point policy rate increase at the Fed's December 8-9 meeting, up from about 67% on Thursday. Traders now also see the next and final rate increase coming earlier, in April instead of June, as the central bank battles inflation that has been running above its 2% target for more than five years.

items.title: US consumer sentiment improves in November; worries about AI bubble emerge By Reuters
items.excerpt: WASHINGTON, Nov 6 (Reuters) - US consumer sentiment improved in early November, though concerns over the higher cost of living remained and households worried about a possible artificial intelligence bubble, a survey showed on Friday. The University of Michigan’s Surveys of Consumers said its Consumer Sentiment Index rose to 51.0 this month from a final reading of 48.0 in October. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast the index unchanged at 48.0. The improvement in sentiment was concentrated among respondents identifying as Independents. The survey was conducted between October 20 and November 2. Anger over inflation stemming from tariffs on imports and the US-Israeli war resulted in President Donald Trump’s Republican Party losing control of Congress to Democrats in the midterm elections on Tuesday. "While sentiment lifted for lower- and middle-wealth consumers, it fell 5% for those with the largest stock portfolios in the wake of a relatively turbulent period in stock markets," said Joanne Hsu, the director of the Surveys of Consumers. ... The survey’s measure of consumer expectations for inflation over the next year fell to 4.3% from 4.7% last month. Consumers’ expectations for inflation over the next five years dipped to 3.4% from 3.5% in October.

items.title: Markets fret over growth and inflation despite easing oil prices By Reuters
items.excerpt: LONDON, Nov 6 (Reuters) - Uncertainty over the growth outlook and expectations that inflation will remain elevated next year are weighing on global markets, even as hopes of a de-escalation in the Iran war have eased oil prices. Government borrowing costs have ... The combination is fuelling concern that inflation could stay high even as growth slows, although the Democratic victory in US midterm elections has raised hopes for an eventual end to the Iran war. OIL STILL HIGH Oil has fallen 15% this week to just below $100 a barrel. But analysts warn that any resolution to the Iran war remains uncertain, leaving scope for prices to rise again. Oil is still up 64% this year, while natural gas remains nearly three times its level at the start of 2026. That backdrop is keeping near-term inflation expectations elevated and reinforcing concerns that price pressures could persist as growth slows, forcing central banks to raise interest rates further. The University of Michigan’s measure of one-year US inflation expectations edged up to 4.7% in October from 4.6% in September and ​3.4% in February. Market measures of long-term inflation expectations remain above 2% in the euro zone and the US, and above 3% in Britain. Higher energy costs add to inflation while also weighing on growth by increasing transport, manufacturing and household expenses.

So far, Democrats have won 253 House seats compared to Republicans’ 157, with 25 races still undecided. In Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom has added to his narrow lead over incumbent Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith. He’s currently ahead by more than 1,800 votes as election officials process provisional ballots and late-arriving mail ballots. Colom would be the first Black senator from Mississippi since Blanche K. Bruce was elected in 1875, during the Reconstruction era. In Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola narrowly leads incumbent Republican Senator Dan Sullivan by just over 600 votes, though a quarter of ballots remain to be counted. If Democrats win Alaska and Mississippi, their Senate caucus will grow to 56 members. ## Incoming Freshman Senators Call for New Leadership to Replace Top Democrat Chuck Schumer Nov 06, 2026 There are growing calls for new leadership to challenge Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer and House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries. Senators-elect Peggy Flanagan, Troy Jackson, Abdul El-Sayed, Juliana Stratton and Adam Hamilton have all said they won’t support Schumer, as has Senate candidate Scott Colom in Mississippi. This is Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed speaking with The Bulwark after Tuesday’s election. > Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed: “I’ve had conversations, obviously, with Senator Schumer in the context of this race. I’ve been clear: I want new leadership, and I want leadership that is focused on getting money out of politics, putting money in your pocket, passing Medicare for All. But at the end of the day, it’s a choice between two or more options, so I want to see who else is willing to put their hat in the ring.” On Wednesday, CNN’s Manu Raju asked Senator Schumer about growing calls for him to step down as Senate Democratic leader. > Manu Raju: “How do you deal with those candidates who won who say they’re not going to vote for you?” > Sen. Chuck Schumer: “Look” — > Manu Raju: “Adam Hamilton, Troy Jackson, Abdul El-Sayed?” > Sen. Chuck Schumer: “OK, again, to repeat the answer: The issue is not me. I’ll be reelected as majority leader.” In Texas, Senator-elect James Talarico has refused to commit to backing Schumer. Talarico is also calling on fellow Democrats to abolish the filibuster, a rule that effectively requires 60 of the Senate’s 100 members to pass legislation. Talarico spoke with NBC News. > Sen.-elect James Talarico: “I believe that the majority has the right to govern in this country. And the filibuster, which is not in the Constitution — it’s a Jim Crow relic — it is — it is leading to gridlock.” Meanwhile, an online petition calling on Democrats to reject New York Congressmember Hakeem Jeffries as House speaker in the new Congress has garnered over 830,000 signatures. ... Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth defended the Iran war and lashed out at his critics on Thursday, as the House of Representatives prepares to vote as early as next week on articles of impeachment. The effort to oust Hegseth is being led by Kentucky’s outgoing Republican Congressmember Thomas Massie, who gave Hegseth an ultimatum after Tuesday’s historic losses for Republicans: Resign or be removed by Congress.

items.excerpt: Meghan's estranged father arrested and charged with possessing child sexual abuse materials TAMPA, Fla. (AP) — Thomas Markle, the 82-year-old father of Prince Harry’s wife Meghan, has been arrested by federal agents in Florida and charged with possessing child sexual abuse material in California. Thomas Markle was released after a court appearance in Tampa. Authorities say a search of storage units in the Los Angeles area turned up dozens of items. There was no immediate comment from his lawyer. Meghan Markle had recently said she's “deeply distressed” about allegations that a collection of child sexual abuse images were found at her father’s former home in the Philippines. 25 years after 'Britney,' 5 new Britney Spears songs showcase a pop icon at a transformative moment NEW YORK (AP) — Britney Spears' 2001 self-titled album ‘Britney' marked a pivotal moment in her career. At 19, she was already a global icon, transitioning from teen pop to a more mature sound. The album, certified quadruple platinum, showcased her evolution with hits like “I'm a Slave 4 U.” On Friday, Legacy Recordings releases the “Britney (25th Anniversary Edition).” It features five previously unreleased tracks and two new remixes. These songs add depth to her legacy, reflecting themes of autonomy and self-definition. Fans can revisit the album, exploring its impact and Spears’ journey from adolescence to adulthood. Awkwafina digs into her culinary roots to try something a little crazy: Open a restaurant NEW YORK (AP) — Awkwafina has taken a surprising turn in her career by diving into the culinary world. Her new Apple TV series, “Awkwafina: The Unlikely Cook,” follows her journey from a novice cook to opening her own restaurant. The show, premiering Friday, captures her learning experiences, from making stir-fry to mastering Peking duck. Awkwafina was born Nora Lum and comes from a family with a rich restaurant history. They opened the New York City eatery Lum's. Her journey reconnects her with her roots and honors her family. The series also highlights a trend of Asian Americans returning to the restaurant industry, defying their parents' expectations. In 'Being Heumann,' Siân Heder and Ruth Madeley channel the spirit of a disability rights pioneer NEW YORK (AP) — Siân Heder's follow-up to the best picture-winning “CODA” chronicles the disability rights pioneer Judy Heumann. Heumann died at the age of 75 in 2023 while Heder was developing the movie with her. She resolved to push on with the project to honor Heumann and try to bring some of her accessibility gains to the movie industry. Characters with disabilities remain extremely uncommon in Hollywood productions, and big-screen biopics like “Being Heumann” are even more seldom. “Being Heumann,” starring Ruth Madeley as Heumann, features the largest ensemble ever of performers with disabilities. Oscar-winning Chilean filmmaker Sebastián Lelio dies at 52 SANTIAGO, Chile (AP) — Oscar-winning Chilean filmmaker Sebastián Lelio has died in Santiago, Chile, at 52. His family announced his death Friday on Instagram, citing health reasons but not specifying the cause. Lelio was known for his groundbreaking film “A Fantastic Woman,” which portrayed a transgender woman and won the Academy Award for best international film. ... In ‘Possible Love,’ a South Korean auteur returns with a story of marriage, labor and class VENICE, Italy (AP) — South Korean filmmaker Lee Chang-dong's latest film, “Possible Love,” is now streaming on Netflix. The film explores the impact of mass layoffs in South Korea, inspired by the 2009 Ssangyong Motor Co. incident. The story follows a laid-off autoworker and his wife, played by Jeon Do-yeon, who agrees to be followed by a well-off documentary filmmaker. The film, which premiered at the Venice Film Festival where it won the runner-up prize, is South Korea’s submission for the Academy Awards. Lee last directed “Burning,” which was short-listed for an Oscar in 2018. Lady Gaga, Shakira, Jack White and Boy George lead the 2027 Songwriters Hall of Fame nominees NEW YORK (AP) — Lady Gaga, Shakira, Pink, Boy George, Jack White, Sia, Vince Gill, Ne-Yo, Blondie’s Debbie Harry and Chris Stein are among the impressive list of nominees for the 2027 Songwriters Hall of Fame class. Also on the ballot are America’s Gerry Beckley and Dewey Bunnell, Grandmaster Melle Mel as well as members of ZZ Top and War. Eligible voting members have until midnight Eastern Standard Time on Dec. 14 to turn in ballots with their choices of up to three nominees from the songwriter category and up to three from the performing-songwriter category. The 2027 inductees will be announced in early 2027. Last year's class included Taylor Swift, Kiss’s Gene Simmons, Paul Stanley and more.
